schools.summary: Gill reads the gift as a re-clothing so that David might appear at court as a prince, and the covenant as a mutual bond that gave him a friend at court for life.
Henry traces the friendship to David's speech, presses the detail that the clothes came off Jonathan's own back, and turns the stripping into a figure of Christ.
Clarke takes the ancients' maxim that a friend is another self, makes David generalissimo, and notes that the Greek version omits these five verses.
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both compare the exchange of armour in the Iliad; Ellicott dwells on the power David had to disarm the jealousy of men he was overtaking.

sides.position: Generalissimo, what a later age would call field marshal
One of the commanders set over the men of war
Not the generalship, which Abner held, but perhaps the lifeguard, or precedence out of turn

outliers.note: Alone in reading the stripping as a figure of Christ, who went further than Jonathan in putting on our rags while Jonathan did not put on David's.

themes: knit with the soul of David
Jonathan stripped himself of the robe
David behaved himself wisely
accepted in the sight of all the people
1.pericope_label: The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David

schools.summary: Gill gives the eyeing both senses, a sour look and a watching for treason, with the Targum making it a lying in wait.
Henry has the poet more just than wise, holds that a prince should be above noticing a slight when the public glory is meant, and sets the harp against the javelin.

Clarke makes the song a reckoning of odds rather than of the slain, identifies the instruments as sistrums, and reads the fit as feigned family prayer; Wesley dates the relapse to the day after the envy.
Keil and Delitzsch report Thenius on the section's source and settle the verb as raving; Ellicott dates the triumph to the end of the campaign and traces the madness into a new phase.

debates.question: Was the prophesying a real fit or a pretence?

sides.position: Raving, the word not meaning prophecy here, and the conjugation never used of true prophecy
Feigned devotion, since the conjugation can mean to feign: family prayer put on to disarm David
A religious ecstasy assumed to decoy David within reach, with a divine impulse to be pleaded afterwards

outliers.note: Alone in citing Justin for the age when kings carried a spear instead of a diadem and spears were worshipped as images of the gods.

themes: Saul hath slain his thousands
what can he have more but the kingdom?
the evil spirit from God came upon Saul
I will smite David even to the wall
6.pericope_label: Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands

schools.summary: Gill grounds the fear in the plain fact that the Lord was with David, reports the Targum and the reading which takes it of the Holy Ghost, and makes the wise behaviour a type of Christ.
Henry allows the fear may have been partly pretence, compares Herod's awe of John, and makes wise behaviour the way to be both feared and loved.
Clarke calls the command of a thousand a pretence of honour to rid the court of an envied man; Wesley adds the wish to expose him to hazards.
Ellicott makes the fear the king's clearest-sighted moment and reads the naming of Israel and Judah as a mark of the compiler's date; Keil and Delitzsch describe the prospering of his enterprises.

debates.question: Why was David removed from the court?

sides.position: Under a pretence of honour, to rid the court of the object of its envy
For fear of assassination, and chiefly to expose him to hazards
To get him from under the king's eye and away from the courtiers, which was badly judged, since it gave him the people

outliers.note: Alone in inferring from the naming of Israel and Judah together that the compiler wrote after the separation under Rehoboam.

themes: Saul was afraid of David
he made him his captain over a thousand
David behaved himself wisely in all his ways
all Israel and Judah loved David
12.pericope_label: Saul was afraid of David; all Israel and Judah loved him

schools.summary: Gill says in a line that the offer was made not in good will but to lay a snare.
Clarke takes from Calmet the rule that Hebrew wars were the Lord's only while waged by his express orders; Wesley reads the answer as asking how little a life was worth to buy a king's daughter.
Keil and Delitzsch render the question of condition in life and admit the phrase is difficult; Ellicott lists three readings and follows Ewald and Lange in making it a question about the family.

debates.question: What does the question about his life mean?

sides.position: What his condition in life amounted to
What his family or relations were, following Ewald and Lange
How little his life was worth to be the purchase of a king's daughter

outliers.note: Alone in drawing the line at which a war ceases to be the Lord's, namely when worldly ambition mingles with it and it becomes a war of lust and profanity.

themes: be thou valiant for me, and fight the LORD's battles
let not mine hand be upon him
who am I? and what is my life?
she was given unto Adriel
17.pericope_label: Behold my elder daughter Merab, her will I give thee to wife

schools.summary: Gill notes the irony that the woman meant for a snare became the means of David's escape, and explains why the courtiers had to be used at all.
Clarke says the condition of a hundred Philistines was already fixed in the king's mind, and that he expected the attempt to kill him.

Keil and Delitzsch explain the earlier breach of promise by Merab's want of love and take the plea of poverty as sincere; Ellicott prefers in this second way and hears a soldier of fortune in the reply.

debates.question: What was the snare to consist of?

sides.position: The condition that would be proposed, which was to prove his ruin
A hundred Philistines, an attempt he must necessarily perish in
A plot whose method David himself afterwards used against Uriah

outliers.note: Alone in suggesting that this plot, once it became public knowledge, is where David found the method he used against Uriah at the siege of Rabbah.

themes: Michal Saul's daughter loved David
that she may be a snare to him
the king hath delight in thee
I am a poor man, and lightly esteemed
20.pericope_label: Michal loved David; I will give him her, that she may be a snare to him

schools.summary: Gill keeps the two hundred of the Hebrew, stresses that the verb is singular, and reads the exploit as obedience and zeal for God and country.
Clarke explains the tokens as proof that the slain were uncircumcised, reports a like custom among the Abyssinians, and prefers the smaller number; Wesley makes the doubling deliberate.

Keil and Delitzsch observe that no dowry was asked and state the murderous design plainly; Ellicott passes on the reading that the tokens betray a suspicious mind and enters the chapter's one moral protest.

debates.question: Was the number one hundred or two hundred?

sides.position: One hundred, since the bargain was for that and David later said so himself
Two hundred, a hundred more than required, the Greek version notwithstanding
Two hundred, doubled on purpose to bind the king to his promise

outliers.note: Alone in protesting at the age itself, that such a bargain offered, accepted and overpaid shows how half-barbarous the times were.

themes: an hundred foreskins of the Philistines
to be avenged of the king's enemies
Saul thought to make David fall
Saul gave him Michal his daughter
24.pericope_label: The king desireth not any dowry, but an hundred foreskins of the Philistines

schools.summary: Gill lists the evidence by which the king came to know it, adds the Targum's phrasing, and alone answers the rabbinic plea about the newly married man.
Clarke and Wesley both put the Philistine attack down to revenge for earlier losses, Clarke noting that nothing else of the war is known.
Ellicott makes the recognition the effect of the last enterprise and reports the rabbinic explanation; Keil and Delitzsch locate the occasion of the enmity in David's unbroken success.

debates.question: Why did the Philistine princes come out at this moment?

sides.position: Revenge, provoked by their losses and by the killing of two hundred of their men
They counted on the Hebrew law exempting a newly married man from war for a year

outliers.note: Alone in answering the exemption argument, that the law applied to the commanded war against the seven nations and not to a voluntary one.

themes: Saul saw that the LORD was with David
Saul became David's enemy continually
the princes of the Philistines went forth
his name was much set by
28.pericope_label: Saul became David's enemy continually; his name was much set by
